title: Study on the Effect of Activated Carbon on AnMBR for Treating Saline Acidic Selenium-Containing Wastewater
description: This study investigates the use of an anaerobic membrane bioreactor (AnMBR) to treat acidic (pH=3) selenium-containing wastewater with high salinity. Actual beer wastewater was used as the carbon source. Two reactor configurations were compared: a control without activated carbon (B-MBR) and a test reactor with activated carbon (C-MBR). The goal was to understand how activated carbon affects selenium removal, microbial community responses, and membrane fouling.Results showed that salinity changes did not significantly impact selenium removal, with over 97% soluble selenium removed across all stages. However, salinity clearly reduced COD removal efficiency and accelerated membrane fouling. Adding activated carbon reduced the membrane fouling rate by about 30%. Selenium was reduced to hexagonal selenium nanoparticles (SeNPs) wrapped in extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), with a higher proportion of SeNPs observed in the C-MBR.Key selenium-reducing bacteria included Dechloromonas, Pseudomonas, and Thauera. Functional genes such as SerABC and NapAB were dominant for selenate (Se(VI)) reduction, while FrdABC, NirB, and TrxB drove selenite (Se(IV)) reduction.This study provides a theoretical basis for using activated carbon to enhance AnMBR performance in treating acidic, saline selenium-laden wastewater. Future work may optimize activated carbon dosing to improve shock resistance and fouling control.
